Elie Benoist
ā-lē' ben-wah'
n. (Elie Benoist, 1640–1728, pastor of Alençon, historian of the Edict of Nantes)
Hebrew Eliyahu, the LORD is God, through French Élie; Benoist, the French form of Benedictus, blessed.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Elie Benoist was pastor at Alençon in Normandy until the Revocation drove him out in 1685, and he spent the remaining forty-three years of his life at Delft, pastor of the Walloon church there. His monument is the Histoire de l'Édit de Nantes, published at Delft in five quarto volumes between 1693 and 1695: a documentary history of the French Reformed churches from the Edict of 1598 to its revocation, built out of the edicts, declarations, judgments, synodal acts and local records that he and his correspondents could gather. He wrote it while the events were within living memory and while the documents still existed, many of which were later destroyed, and it remains a primary source for the whole period that no later historian can bypass. He understood what he was doing: the churches had been abolished by law and their very existence was being written out of the record, and a history with the documents printed in it could not be unsaid. “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a document as a written instrument conveying information or proof, and a record as a register, an authentic account of facts.

expand to see more

DOC'UMENT, n. A written instrument conveying information; anything serving as proof or evidence.

REC'ORD, n. A register; an authentic or official copy of any writing; a memorial.

HIS'TORY, n. An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states, in the order of time.

GENERA'TION, n. A single succession of living beings in natural descent; the people of the same period.

Modern Corruption

The exiled pastor who wrote the documentary history of the churches France abolished.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a methodological fashion that would discount Benoist because he was a party to what he described: the victim, it is said, cannot be the historian. The objection is worth less than it sounds. Benoist printed the documents, including the crown's own edicts and declarations, and invited his readers to weigh them; a history that prints its evidence is more easily checked than one that summarises it.

The principle to recover is that the church is commanded to keep and hand on the record of God's dealings with it, including the record of its sufferings: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). The psalmist's confidence is that nothing is lost in the keeping: “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?” (Psa 56:8).

Usage

"“This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18) — five volumes at Delft, 1693 to 1695."

"“We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) — a history written from the documents."

"“Thou tellest my wanderings” (Psa 56:8) — the churches France legislated out of existence."
